findings.description: storage_encrypted is set to false, so the MySQL database stores all data, including customer records in the EMPLOYEES table and the admin credentials, unencrypted on disk and in snapshots.

publicly_accessible = true assigns the RDS instance a public IP address, exposing the MySQL listener (port 3306) to the internet. Combined with the hard-coded admin username and the password supplied via var.password, this creates a directly reachable brute-force/credential-stuffing target.

The user_data script writes the live RDS endpoint, admin username and var.password (DB_PASSWORD) into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc on the instance. Instance user data and any image derived from it expose the database admin password in plaintext to anyone with EC2 metadata or filesystem access, and the password is also readable in Terraform state.

The master username is the fixed value "admin" rather than a less predictable identity, and the instance uses the same single privileged account for the application, weakening credential hygiene for an internet-exposed database.

The policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*", giving the EC2 instance (and anyone who compromises it or reads its metadata credentials) full control over all S3 buckets, EC2 instances and RDS databases in the account, including the ability to delete or exfiltrate data and escalate privileges.

The database security group is declared with no inline ingress rules and is only populated by the associated aws_security_group_rule, meaning all access control depends entirely on that separate rule set; the rule that does exist permits 0.0.0.0/0-equivalent MySQL traffic when combined with publicly_accessible. This block should be reviewed together with catalog_db_inbound.

Ingress to port 3306 is allowed from the entire VPC CIDR block (aws_vpc.portal_vpc.cidr_block) rather than a tightly scoped application security group. Combined with publicly_accessible = true on the DB, any resource in the VPC—including the compromise-prone web server—can reach the database on the MySQL port.

The database security group permits all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on all protocols and ports, which lets a compromised database instance initiate arbitrary outbound connections for data exfiltration or command-and-control.

The configuration publishes the application server's public DNS name as an output, advertising the internet-facing host that fronts the publicly accessible, credential-bearing database to anyone who can read the configuration or state.
The database endpoint (host and port ending in the MySQL service port) is emitted as an output, revealing the exact address of the publicly accessible database for attackers to target.

The instance profile attaches catalog_app_role, whose attached policy grants full account-wide s3:*/ec2:*/rds:* permissions, to the EC2 web server; anyone reaching the instance via its exposed services or metadata endpoint inherits those broad credentials.
